author: pgaudet
body:
From @ValWood in https://github.com/geneontology/go-announcements/issues/1050#issuecomment-3618242135

> Sometimes I am not sure what I can annotate to instead.
For example
https://www.pombase.org/gene/SPCC320.14
serine racemase
interconverts between L and D serine. I annotated this to "serine metabolic process" and I can't think of an alternative. biosynthesis and catabolism don't work...
(actually aI managed to do all the others, its only this one I wasn't sure what to do)

author: rozaru
body: I am having some problems in finding a suitable replacement for the obsolete GO terms (one is the same issue as Val mentioned above). --- protein r catalyses the first 3 steps in the pyrimidine ribonucleotide biosynthetic process. It uses L-glutamine as starting material to provide a carbamoyl group (Panel A in Fig below) Currently, it is annotated with the GO term **glutamine metabolic process** which is going to be obsolete. Option 1: remove the GO term and no replacement with related glutamine GO term Option 2: replace with a related glutamine GO term, the only option is L-glutamine catabolic process but L-glutamine is converted to L-glutamate so not a catabolic process. These are the GO terms available: ``` glutamine metabolic process |__ammonia assimilation cycle |__cyclization of glutamine involved in intein-mediated protein splicing |__glutamine biosynthetic process | |__L-glutamine biosynthetic process |__L-glutamine catabolic process ``` --- Alat is a transaminase that catalyses the reversible reaction L-alanine + 2-oxoglutarate = pyruvate + L-glutamate. Due to the participants in the reactions it can be involved in multiple pathways (Panel A in Fig below). Currently, it is annotated to **L-alanine metabolic process**. Based on the information in the paper I could annotated with L-alanine biosynthetic process (although in this case it is a 1 step process) and L-alanine catabolic process, by transamination (again a 1 step process). Is the above the best way to do the annotation? At the time I used L-alanine metabolic process as I thought it would cover what was going on better. An issue with L-alanine metabolism is that among the children there are a few that are a 1 step process: ``` L-alanine metabolic process |__beta-alanine catabolic process to L-alanine (1 STEP REACTION) |__L-alanine biosynthetic process | |__L-alanine biosynthetic process from pyruvate (1 STEP REACTION) | |__L-alanine biosynthetic process via ornithine (1 STEP REACTION) |__L-alanine catabolic process |__anaerobic L-alanine catabolic process |__L-alanine catabolic process, by transamination (1 STEP REACTION) |__L-alanine oxidation to D-lactate and ammonia |__L-alanine oxidation to pyruvate via D-alanine ``` --- Srr is a serine racemase that can catalyse the conversion of L-ser to D-ser and L/S-ser to pyruvate and ammonia (Panel C in Fig below). Currently, it has **L-serine metabolic process** and **D-serine metabolic process annotation**. The reaction to make and convert both residues are 1 step processes this is why in the end I used a metabolic process term. Is it appropriate to use D-serine catabolic process, D-serine biosynthetic process and L-serine catabolic process terms? ``` D-serine metabolic process |__D-serine biosynthetic process |__D-serine catabolic process L-serine metabolic process |__cysteine biosynthetic process from serine |__glycine biosynthetic process from serine |__L-serine biosynthetic process |__L-serine catabolic process ```

author: pgaudet
body:
Hi @rozaru 
For case 1, protein r:
> protein r catalyses the first 3 steps in the pyrimidine ribonucleotide biosynthetic process.

I dont see that you need to mention glutamine; clearly the BP is pyrimidine ribonucleotide biosynthetic process.
Is it OK for you to remove mention of glutamine for BP associated with this gene?

author: pgaudet
body:
For case 2, Alat 
> transaminase that catalyses the reversible reaction L-alanine + 2-oxoglutarate = pyruvate + L-glutamate. Due to the participants in the reactions it can be involved in multiple pathways 

I would annotate the various pathways based on individual papers, not solely based on the chemical reaction Alat catalyzes.

author: deustp01
body: Transamination processes function to couple the biosynthesis of one amino acid to the catabolism of another. That's how the biology has evolved, so I don't see a legal term to "fix" annotations of processes like Reactome:R-HSA-8963693 and R-HSA-8964539, currently annotated to GO:0170033 L-amino acid metabolic process. (These are more examples of the cross-term processes that @RLovering highlighted above.)

author: pgaudet
ValWood
body:
> How else does [D-serine biosynthetic process](http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/GO_0070179) happen ?

To be honest, I don't know the purpose of this reaction. From my understanding D-serine is toxic for yeast.
The annotations come from this paper:
https://www.pombase.org/reference/PMID:19640845 (and 2 others)
and I guess I went for metabolic processes because I wasn't sure of the purpose. I haven't included it in a GO-CAM model.

I thought that we didn't want to annotate interconversions to biosynthesis or catabolism?

Interestingly the S. cerevisiae ortholog isn't reported to be a serine racemase
https://www.yeastgenome.org/locus/S000001701

I don't really know what to do with it so "metabolism" seemed safest.

author: pgaudet
body: Looks like there shouldn't be a BP annotation for this gene - not enough data.

author: ValWood
body: I think users would expect to see  it annotated to serine metabolic process. It will place it in the correct slim bin. I agree that we should not annotate to high-level terms, but here we clearly know enough to annotate to serine metabolism....even if we don't quite know why...

author: edwong57
body:
> Hi What should I do with NAGS? PMID:21757002, this is just a TAS but how should I handle an enzyme that catalyses glutamate to N-acetylglutamate (NAG) by the activity of the enzyme NAG synthetase (NAGS). I would look up the references for this reaction but not much point if the metabolism term is not to be used and I am not sure that this would be captured as glutamate catabolism. Thanks Ruth

Hi Ruth, I read a couple of papers, and from those, it seems like NAGS making glutamate into N-actylglutamate (NAG) as a co-activator of CPS-I, which is involved in ureagenesis (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1096719204000046?casa_token=XpOcdyUTuhkAAAAA:FJc4--JADB58wPke8PoxGkj4mCU-sZ7z2cfjt9qDivqtHJ7oKdoj695_eOXCLt1f_ididMxIaA-E). Would a new BP term of "positive regulation of the urea cycle" be appropriate? Or an alternative would be to make an N-Acetyl-Glutamate biosynthetic process term? What are your thoughts about these ideas?

author: deustp01
body:
> Would a new BP term of "positive regulation of the urea cycle" be appropriate?

Yes - that's the well-known role of NAGS. More words and references [here,](https://reactome.org/PathwayBrowser/#/R-HSA-70542) including IMP evidence for the function of the human protein.

author: edwong57
body:
> Also how should I capture this information: hNit2/ω-amidase plays a crucial metabolic role by catalyzing the hydrolysis of α-ketoglutaramate (the α-keto analog of glutamine) and α-ketosuccinamate (the α-keto analog of asparagine), yielding α-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate, respectively. PMID: 22674578 Thanks

From this [figure](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00726-015-2115-x), and a couple of other papers, it seems like this enzyme is part of two different two-step pathways (Glutaminase II and asparaginase II), with L-glutamine or L-asparagine as the starting point. 

The pathway involving aparagine seems to be part of this Metacyc pathway - [MetaCyc:PWY-4002 ](http://vm-trypanocyc.toulouse.inra.fr/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=NIL&object=PWY-4002&redirect=T). There's a BP term, 'L-asparagine catabolic process via 2-oxosuccinamate', GO:0033346 which you could use, I think. 

For the L-glutamine->α-ketoglutaramate-> α-ketoglutarate, would the term 'L-glutamine catabolic process' work? Or, maybe a new child term of L-glutamine catabolic process that is similar to GO:0033346?

author: edwong57
body:
> Also how to capture the remethylation of homocysteine to form methionine PMID: 17369066 by MTRR, (and MetE, MetH PMID:8572314) as this doesn’t seem to be homocysteine catabolism?
> 
> Thanks
> 
> Ruth

It looks like there should be a new process term created - L-methionine salvage from L-homocysteine - [MetaCyc:ADENOSYLHOMOCYSCAT-PWY](http://vm-trypanocyc.toulouse.inra.fr/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=PATHWAY&object=ADENOSYLHOMOCYSCAT-PWY). Does this pathway seem correct to you? Right now, it is crossreferenced to GO:0019510 S-adendosylhomocysteine catabolic process, but I am not sure that is correct.

body:
> how to capture the remethylation of homocysteine to form methionine

Another use case for a BP metabolism category "interconversion" for processes that are not really either synthetic nor catabolic?

author: pgaudet
body:
Hi @shurjenw 

Thank you for your question. We propose to obsolete many of the terms containing the word 'metabolic process'. We will of course keep the children 'biosynthetic' and 'catabolic process. 

The new structure will look like this: 

amino acid metabolic process (keep as a general grouping term)
** L-amino acid metabolic process (keep as a general grouping term)
*** L-amino acid biosynthetic process
**** L-proteinogenic amino acid biosynthetic process
***** L-alanine amino acid biosynthetic process
***** L-asparigine acid biosynthetic process
***** L-aspartate amino acid biosynthetic process
***** etc
*** amino acid catabolic process
**** L-proteinogenic amino acid catabolic process
***** L-alanine amino acid catabolic process
***** L-asparigine acid catabolic process
***** L-aspartate amino acid catabolic process


Is this clearer ?

author: rozaru
body:
**Hydroxyproline metabolism**

For mammals there is a GO term GO:0019470 trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline catabolic process but the first step (RHEA:52512) has no MF term.
PMID:25608448 (Figure 1 compare proline and hydroxyproline degradation pathway)

Maybe we could have a more general term hydroxy-L-proline catabolic process without mentioning the exact position of the hydroxy group.

@pgaudet @edwong57 @sjm41

author: deustp01
body:
> but the first step (RHEA:52512) has no MF term.

[Reactome](https://reactome.org/PathwayBrowser/#/R-HSA-895581) has UniProt:Q9UF12 PRODH2 enabling this reaction with MF [GO:0004657](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/QuickGO/GTerm?id=GO:0004657) proline dehydrogenase activity. The Reactome reaction is cross-referenced to RHEA:52513 to indicate the physiological direction. Neither GO nor the UniProt entry for PRODH2 seems to be concerned about the distinction between proline and hydroxyproline as a substrate for the reaction. Should the GO definition be broadened to to accommodate both? An oddity is that the parallel action of PRODH on proline is annotated by UniProt (following Reactome) as mediating a more general MF, [GO:0016649](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/QuickGO/term/GO:0016649)
oxidoreductase activity, acting on the CH-NH group of donors, quinone or similar compound as acceptor.

Would it be better to apply the same MF to both reactions - GO:0004657 looks good to me but this is open for discussion - associate that MF with RHEA:52512 and its children, edit the GO MF definition, and edit the Reactome annotations, to make all ofthis consistent?

author: sjm41
body: > Maybe we could have a more general term hydroxy-L-proline catabolic process without mentioning the exact position of the hydroxy group. That would be consistent with how MetaCyc handles this: they have a class "hydroxy-L-proline Degradation" with 3 specific variant pathways: trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline degradation (PWY-7515) - not in GO trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline degradation I (HYDROXYPRODEG-PWY) - currently an xref on GO:0019470 trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline degradation II (PWY-5159) - currently an xref on GO:0019470 So we could broaden the label and def of GO:0019470 and have all 3 MetaCyc xrefs as narrowMatch. New ticket?
